claim: The identification has been institutionally dismissed rather than evidentially refuted. (Owner's position 2, transcribed verbatim; 'the identification' is the identification of the Rigvedic forts with Indus-period sites.)
notes: A HISTORIOGRAPHICAL claim, not an archaeological one: it is about how a discipline treated a proposal, and it is answerable by publication history, review record, citation trail and the institutional positions of those who closed the question. Enters INHERITED-UNVERIFIED and is NOT RESOLVED HERE, by instruction. It is also an argument from an absence - the absence of an evidential refutation - so the negative-evidence standard at constitution section 6 governs it: before it is argued from, the record must state what a refutation would have looked like, who would have produced it, where it would have been published, the probability it was produced, the probability it survived and is accessible, and whether we would recognise it if we saw it; and the absence must then be typed as one of NOT PRODUCED, NOT PRESERVED, NOT EXCAVATED, NOT PUBLISHED, NOT ACCESSIBLE, NOT RECOGNISED, DOCUMENTED DESTRUCTION or ABSENT DESPITE ADEQUATE SEARCH. None of that is done here, so the position is untested rather than strong. Two failure modes are on record against it, in both directions: accepting it because it is anti-institutional and corrective would be the preferred-counter-narrative failure; dropping it as 'not archaeology' would be the prestige failure. A NAMED ANALOGY, TYPED AS AN ANALOGY AND NOT AS SUPPORT: who-writes-the-textbook.html reports that injuries on the Harappa bones recognised by Anthropological Survey of India researchers decades earlier 'remained largely uninvestigated', because 'most research until now had been directed at arguing that the injuries on the bones were not due to an Aryan invasion'. That is a documented case of the mechanism this position alleges, in a neighbouring question, and it is a reason to TEST the position and not a reason to accept it - a mechanism existing somewhere is not the mechanism operating here. The analogy is recorded so that it is argued with rather than assumed, and BR-J-001 states that no support flows from it. Step 11 (current standing, run against citation inertia) is the instrument that would test this, and it has not been run. CORRECTION 2026-09-08, adversarial review findings F-12 and F-1: the analogy was previously offered as 'evidenced in a neighbouring case' without being typed, and the page it rests on was misquoted elsewhere in this unit (see MDO-OCC-014); the quotation here is checked against who-writes-the-textbook.html at SRC-089.
